findings.location: crates/foundry-acceptance/src/support/rail_reading.rs NAV_PROBE (the readMember half, functions inTheFocusOrder, faded, centreInViewport, hitsItsOwnCentre, visibleNow) against FOCUS_PROBE (the same five functions declared again)
findings.obligation: nw-code-craftsmanship rule 2 and rule 10 (one owner per fact; two units sharing an algorithm get one owner) and nw-code-design-oo section 1 rule 4, applied to the oracle support this module exists to be: the file's own module doc states the law it must keep - 'The same test decides the visible of a keyboard stop, so a walk and a sweep cannot disagree about what the operator can see' - and that is exactly what the module was created to guarantee after three readings of the rail had drifted apart
findings.observation: The definition of visible is declared TWICE, as two literal copies inside two JavaScript string constants in one file: NAV_PROBE carries inTheFocusOrder, faded, centreInViewport, hitsItsOwnCentre and visibleNow, and FOCUS_PROBE carries five functions of the same names and the same bodies. Nothing couples them: a future change to the clip-aware half - a fourth hiding mechanism, content-visibility, a different hit-test rule - can be made in one string and leave the other on the old reading, and then the Tab walk and the member sweep DO disagree about what the operator can see while both stay green. The risk is not hypothetical for this very file: commit 37f2c8a had to correct the hit test ('counts only the member or its descendants') and had to correct it in both copies. The duplication is the open advisory the S2 oracle review raised and left non-blocking; I confirm it first-hand and add that the module doc currently claims a guarantee the code does not provide. No behaviour is wrong today: I read both copies line by line and they agree at 2d473dc.
findings.remediation: Give the visibility reading one owner: declare the five functions once in a Rust const (for example VISIBILITY_HELPERS_JS) and build NAV_PROBE and FOCUS_PROBE by concatenating that const with the probe-specific tail, so one edit reaches both probes; or have the focus probe call the member reading rather than redeclare it. Then either keep the module doc's sentence as a fact or, if the two must stay apart, say in the doc that they are two copies and what keeps them equal.

findings.location: crates/foundry-acceptance/src/steps/feature_nav_icon_rail.rs, then_each_focused_icon_reveals_its_name, the wrong_word arm (the comparison stop[labelText] != destination, where destination is stop[text])
findings.obligation: nw-sc-review-dimensions Dimension 2, circular verification: an assertion must be able to fail on a wrong product. The acceptance row for P3 promises that the revealed word 'is the name of the place that icon opens', which is a claim about the WORD against the DESTINATION, not about one DOM text node against itself
findings.observation: destination comes from stop[text] = el.textContent.trim() of the rail member, and the compared value is stop[labelText] = label.textContent.trim() of the span INSIDE that member. The member's only text node is that span's (the glyph is an SVG with no <title>, by design), so the two sides are two readings of the SAME text node and the arm cannot fail on a wrong or swapped word - it can only fail if a second text node appears in the item (the 'Home Home' drift the sidebar comment warns about), which is a different and much weaker claim than the one its failure message makes ('the word a focused icon reveals is not the name of the place it opens'). The destination-name promise is NOT left unobserved: assert_rail_offers compares the BROWSER-computed accessible-name set against the owed set derived from the store's rights, and the same step's missed arm compares the walked stops against that owed set, so the slice's name coverage is sound. This arm alone is the weak one.
findings.remediation: Compare the revealed label against the expectation that does not come from the same node: either match stop[labelText] against the owed destination name the walk was matched on (owed_destinations), or carry the member's accessible name into the focus probe and compare the revealed word with it; keep the existing second-text-node guard, but say in the message what it actually catches.

findings.location: crates/foundry-app/templates/partials/sidebar.html lines 32-46 (the seven inline SVG wrappers on Home, Board, Settings, Keyboard shortcuts, Integrations, Instance admin and the Sign out button) and docs/feature/nav-collapse-icon-rail/architecture.md, the sidebar__item reuse record that rejected an Askama macro
findings.obligation: nw-code-craftsmanship rule 10 (two units sharing a literal set get one named owner) and nw-code-design-oo section 6 (two units that agree on a literal get one owner), read against the accessibility rules the wrapper carries: the template's own comment makes aria-hidden=true, focusable=false and the absence of a <title> load-bearing for the accessible name and for the tab order
findings.observation: The nine-attribute wrapper class=sidebar__icon aria-hidden=true focusable=false viewBox=0 0 24 24 fill=none stroke=currentColor stroke-width=2 stroke-linecap=round stroke-linejoin=round is written out seven times; only the shape children differ. The design record considered and rejected an Askama macro on the ground that seven literal rows 'would gain an indirection and a per-icon branch without removing a decision' - but each row re-decides three accessibility facts, and the oracle does not close the drift: an eighth destination added with aria-hidden or focusable omitted still passes every assertion in the lane, because the accessible name computed from the label span is unchanged by a nameless SVG and the extra legacy tab stop focusable=false exists to prevent is not observed by walk_the_tab_order in a modern engine. So the per-row duplication is a rule checked at render time in seven places with nothing holding the seven equal. No defect exists today: I read all seven rows and they carry the identical attribute set.
findings.remediation: Either give the wrapper one owner - an Askama macro or a small partial taking only the shape children, so the nine attributes are declared once - or, if the seven literal rows stay (a legitimate design choice), add the missing guard: a check that every svg.sidebar__icon in the rendered rail carries aria-hidden=true and focusable=false and no <title>, in the xtask static-asset layer that already walks templates, or in the icon-rail lane's narrow-shape arm beside the iconPresent reading.
